## The crying with no cause

*One baby in five cries inconsolably through its first months — healthy, well fed, nothing a doctor can find. Seventy years on, the best-supported treatment works only for some babies, some of the time.*

Since paediatrician Morris Wessel's work in the 1950s, colic has meant the "rule of threes": crying or fussing at least three hours a day, three days a week, for three weeks, in an otherwise healthy, well-fed infant [@GutirrezCastrelln2017efficacy]. The modern [Rome IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_process) criteria, the field's consensus rulebook, dropped the stopwatch: prolonged crying without obvious cause, in a thriving infant [@Benninga2016childhood].

The two most rigorous community surveys put the incidence between 5% and 19%, with no link to sex, social class, or feeding type [@Lucassen2001systematic]. Crying peaks around six weeks and fades by three to four months [@GutirrezCastrelln2017efficacy]. "Self-limiting" is cold comfort at 3 a.m. Mothers reporting over twenty minutes of inconsolable crying a day had four times the odds of depressive symptoms after birth ([odds ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odds_ratio) 4.0, 95% [confidence interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval) 2.0–8.1) [@Radesky2013inconsolable]; in a Dutch survey of 3,259 families, 5.6% of parents admitted having smothered, slapped, or shaken their baby because of its crying [@Reijneveld2004infant]. Does anything work?

### The suspect in the gut

For decades the prime suspects were gas, temperament, and anxious parenting; none was convicted [@Zeevenhooven2018infant]. The investigation turned to the [gut microbiota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_gastrointestinal_microbiota) — the trillions of bacteria in a newborn's intestine. In a 65-infant case-control study, colicky babies had elevated faecal [calprotectin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calprotectin) — a protein marking gut inflammation — whatever their feeding mode, plus fewer of the *Bifidobacterium* species thought to keep the infant gut calm [@Rhoads2018infant]. In 118 colicky infants whose stool was sequenced, bacterial groups tracked with crying severity, and the baseline mix partly predicted who would still cry a month on [@Loughman2021infant]. A stranger lead: children who were colicky babies had five- to six-fold higher odds of [migraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migraine) (odds ratio 6.5, 95% CI 4.6–8.9) in a meta-analysis — some colic may be an early pain syndrome, not a gut problem at all [@Gelfand2015relationship]. The honest summary: mechanisms are plural, evidence suggestive, no single cause established [@Zeevenhooven2018infant].

### Five drops a day

Could topping up the flora help? That hope made a [probiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probiotic) — live bacteria, five oily drops a day — the centre of colic research. The strain is *[Lactobacillus reuteri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limosilactobacillus_reuteri)* DSM 17938: a network meta-analysis of 32 randomised trials covering 2,242 infants ranked it the best-supported of nine treatment approaches, ahead of dietary changes, drugs, herbs, and manipulation [@GutirrezCastrelln2017efficacy; @Anabrees2013probiotics]. The most careful accounting pooled raw data from 345 infants in four double-blind trials: at day 21, probiotic babies cried or fussed 25 minutes less per day (adjusted mean difference −25.4, 95% CI −47.3 to −3.5), with a breastfed [number needed to treat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_needed_to_treat) of just 2.6 [@Sung2018lactobacillus].

### The Australian spoiler

Then Melbourne researchers ran the largest, most rigorous trial yet: 167 infants — crucially, formula-fed as well as breastfed — same strain, same dose, double-blinded, with a validated cry diary [@Sung2014treating]. The probiotic failed. At one month the treated babies actually fussed *more* than the placebo group (49 minutes a day, 95% CI 8–90), the excess concentrated in formula-fed infants, with no benefit for sleep, maternal mental health, or gut inflammation markers [@Sung2014treating]. The pooled individual-level data reconcile it: benefit in breastfed infants, none in formula-fed — an oddity nobody has explained — plotted in {{figure:colic-treatments}} [@Sung2018lactobacillus]. Europe's paediatric gastroenterology society now recommends the strain for breastfed colicky babies, and nothing for the rest [@Szajewska2023probiotics].

The rest of the treatment shelf is thinner. In systematic reviews the anti-gas staple simethicone showed no benefit, nor did proton pump inhibitors [@Ellwood2020comparison]. A Cochrane review found dietary changes — hypoallergenic formulas, low-allergen maternal diets — backed only by low-quality evidence [@Gordon2018dietary]. Lactase drops made no significant difference in pooled trials (mean difference −17.7 minutes a day, 95% CI −60.8 to 25.5) [@KozowskaJalowska2024effect]. Chiropractic and osteopathic manipulation seemed to reduce crying, but the effect evaporated in trials where parents were blinded [@Dobson2012manipulative].

| What parents try | Best evidence says | Certainty |
|---|---|---|
| *L. reuteri* DSM 17938 (breastfed) | ~25 min/day less crying; NNT 2.6 [@Sung2018lactobacillus] | Moderate |
| *L. reuteri* DSM 17938 (formula-fed) | No benefit; possibly more fussing [@Sung2014treating] | Moderate |
| Dietary change | Possible effect, low-quality trials [@Gordon2018dietary] | Low |
| Lactase drops | No significant effect [@KozowskaJalowska2024effect] | Low |
| Simethicone | No benefit [@Ellwood2020comparison] | Moderate |
| Spinal manipulation | No effect in blinded trials [@Dobson2012manipulative] | Low |

![Three dot-and-whisker rows on one minutes-per-day axis: pooled L. reuteri left of zero, the largest trial right of zero, lactase straddling it.](colic-treatments.png)

**Figure {#colic-treatments}. The best colic treatment helps some babies — and failed its biggest test.** Each whisker is one experiment's verdict in minutes of crying per day versus placebo: the probiotic ahead in pooled trials, behind in the largest, lactase astride zero — three populations, three verdicts, not one average [@Sung2018lactobacillus; @Sung2014treating; @KozowskaJalowska2024effect].

### The verdict, for now

Circle back to that bureaucratic definition: its one unqualified truth is that colic ends, by three to four months, in virtually all infants [@GutirrezCastrelln2017efficacy; @Hjern2020systematic]. Adolescents with a colic history report more indigestion-type complaints (adjusted odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.18–5.25) [@Zeevenhooven2024functional], but long-term evidence shows associations — gut complaints, migraine-type headaches — rather than proven lasting harm [@Indrio2023infantile] — which is why every guideline starts with reassurance, not a prescription [@Ellwood2020comparison]. What would settle it is a trial big enough to say *which* babies the bacteria help and why breast milk matters; until then, the most evidence-based treatment remains the calendar.
